questions.question: Explain three reasons why temperature usually decreases as altitude increases.
questions.expected_answer: First, the atmosphere is heated mainly from below: sunlight passes through the air and is absorbed by the ground, which then heats the air in contact with it by conduction, rising currents and long-wave radiation, so air further from the ground is cooler. Second, air at height is thinner and less dense, with less water vapour, carbon dioxide and dust to absorb and hold heat, so heat escapes more easily; pressure roughly halves every 5.5 km. Third, rising air expands as pressure falls and cools adiabatically. On average temperature falls about 6.5 °C per 1 000 m, the environmental lapse rate.

questions.question: Compare Johannesburg and Cape Town and use the lapse rate to explain why Johannesburg is cooler on average despite its lower latitude.
questions.expected_answer: Johannesburg is at about 26 degrees south and about 1 750 m; Cape Town is at about 34 degrees south at sea level. Johannesburg's mean annual temperature is about 16 °C and Cape Town's about 17 °C, so Johannesburg is slightly cooler although it is closer to the equator. Its height is 1.75 thousand metres; 1.75 × 6.5 ≈ 11.4 °C of cooling, more than enough to outweigh the warming effect of its lower latitude. The estimate overstates the effect because a plateau heats more than free air. The effect shows in July minimums of about 4 °C against 7 °C, frequent frost, and water boiling at about 94 °C.

questions.question: Calculate the expected temperature at the top of a mountain 3 000 m above a coastal town where it is 25 °C, and explain one other effect of altitude on climate.
questions.expected_answer: 3 000 m is 3 thousand-metre units; 3 × 6.5 = 19.5 °C; 25 − 19.5 = 5.5 °C at the summit. Other effects, any one: stronger sunlight and quicker sunburn because there is less air to absorb radiation; larger daily temperature ranges because thin, dry air lets heat in by day and out by night; snow because precipitation falls as ice at low temperatures, as in the Drakensberg and Lesotho; lower air pressure, so water boils below 100 °C and there is less oxygen per breath; zones of vegetation and farming at different heights.
